headline: Amazon's Indigenous Youth Fight Oil With Rap
meta_description: Young Indigenous artists across Ecuador's Amazon are using rap music in native languages to resist extractive industries and protect their territories.
summary_short: Indigenous rappers from Ecuador's Amazon are turning to hip-hop to defend their lands against mining and oil, with one track reaching 400,000 TikTok views in a month.
body:
A new generation of Indigenous artists across Ecuador's Amazon is wielding an unexpected weapon against environmental destruction: rap music performed entirely in native languages. Young rappers including 23-year-old Willan Gualinga (stage name Taki Supay) from the Kichwa community of Sarayaku are channeling centuries of ancestral knowledge into tracks that call out the toll of mining and oil extraction on their ancestral lands. Gualinga's first song, "Let us rise up for the land and for life," draws on elders' stories about Sarayaku's origins while spotlighting modern threats. His peers—including 19-year-old Misa17 from the A'i Cofán community and artists Robenban and Tzitzanu—are reaching audiences far beyond the rainforest. Misa17's track "Ingi Tsampi" (meaning "our forest" in A'ingae) surpassed 400,000 views on TikTok just one month after release, proof that this fusion of ancient language and urban art form resonates globally.

The stakes are staggering. According to MapBiomas data, 71% of mining in Ecuador occurs in the Amazon, with nearly half sitting directly within Indigenous territories. Oil concessions blanket 63% of Amazonian Indigenous lands. By rapping in their native tongues—some on the verge of disappearing—these artists accomplish two things at once: they preserve language and culture while broadcasting urgent warnings to the world. "Through music we can transmit the knowledge of our ancestors and defend the territory," Gualinga explains.

The path remains difficult. Recording studios are scarce in the Amazon, video production costs are prohibitive, and public activism invites retaliation. Yet these young musicians believe art offers something confrontation cannot: the power to inspire change by reaching hearts across borders and awakening a new generation to the Amazon's fight for survival.
quick_facts: Four Indigenous rappers from Ecuador's Amazon perform in native languages threatened with extinction
Misa17's track 'Ingi Tsampi' reached 400,000 TikTok views within one month of release
71% of mining in Ecuador occurs in the Amazon, with 44.5% inside Indigenous territories
Oil concessions cover 63% of land belonging to Amazonian Indigenous peoples and nationalities
Artists like Taki Supay combine ancestral knowledge with hip-hop to resist extractive industries
